'''''Choerospondias axillaris''''', known in English as the '''Nepali hog plum''', is a [[tree]] in the family [[Anacardiaceae]]. It is the sole species in genus '''''Choerospondias'''''. It is native to the [[Himalayas]], [[Indochina]], southern and north-central China, Taiwan, and Japan.<ref name = powo/> It is a common fruit in [[Nepal]] and [[Bhutan]], which is called '''''lapsi''''' (लप्सी) in [[Nepali language|Nepali]], '''''aamli''''' in [[Newar language|Newar]], and '''''phrumchung''''' in eastern [[Bhutan]].

Its fruit is about 3 centimeters long and has a soft whitish sour flesh and green to yellow skin. The fruit is made into [[South Asian pickles|pickles]], fruit tarts, and sour, spicy candy. The tree has long been cultivated for its fruit.<ref name=poudel>{{cite journal |author=Poudel, K. C. |year=2003 |url=http://www.nepjol.info/index.php/HJS/article/viewFile/188/792 |title=Domestication of Lapsi ''Choerospondias axillaris'' (Roxb.) B.L. Burtt & A.W. Hill for fruit production in the middle mountain agroforestry systems of Nepal |journal=Himalayan Journal of Sciences |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=55–58|doi=10.3126/hjs.v1i1.188 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The fruit is nutritious and has a price comparable to the [[mandarin orange]] on the Nepalese market.<ref name=poudel/>

This is a [[deciduous]] tree growing up to 20 meters tall. The smaller branches are purple-brown in color. The compound leaves are up to {{convert|40|cm|abbr=on}} long and divided into 3 to 6 papery oval leaflets each up to {{convert|12|x|4.5|cm|abbr=on}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200012681 |title=''Choerospondias axillaris'' |author1=Tianlu Min |author2=Anders Barfod |work=Flora of China |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden, St. Louis, MO & Harvard University Herbaria, Cambridge, MA |accessdate=2 March 2013}}</ref> The tree is [[plant sexuality|dioecious]], with male and female trees producing different types of [[inflorescence]].<ref name=poudel/> Male flowers occur in long clusters and have curving, brown-veined petals about 3 millimeters long. Female flowers are solitary in leaf axils at the tips of branches. They are larger than the male flowers and yield the edible [[drupe]]. The fallen fruits are consumed and dispersed by [[Sambar (deer)|sambar]] and [[Indian muntjac|barking deer]].<ref>{{cite journal| url=http://dbs.umt.edu/research_labs/maronlab/documents/BrodieetalEcology2009.pdf| journal=Ecology| volume=90| issue=3| pages=688–698| year=2009| title=Functional differences within a guild of tropical mammalian frugivores| author1=Brodie JF| author2=OE Helmy| author3=WY Brockelman| author4=JL Maron| doi=10.1890/08-0111.1| pmid=19341139| bibcode=2009Ecol...90..688B| access-date=2014-12-12| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101230030249/http://dbs.umt.edu/research_labs/maronlab/documents/BrodieetalEcology2009.pdf| archive-date=2010-12-30| url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal| author=Chen, J.| author2=Deng, X.B.| author3=Bai, Z.L.| author4=Yang, Q.| author5=Chen, G.Q.| author6=Liu, Y.| author7=Liu, Z.Q.| name-list-style=amp| year=2002| title=Fruit characteristics and ''Muntiacus muntjac vaginalis'' (Muntjac) visits to individual plants of ''Choerospondias axillaris'' |journal=Biotropica |volume=33 |pages=718–722 |doi=10.1111/j.1744-7429.2001.tb00231.x| s2cid=247704048}}</ref> The fruit is also used in religious ceremonies as an offering.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Food, spices, crafts and resins of Asia: Lapsi, fruit snacks |first=Krishna H. |last=Gautam |publisher=Center for International Forestry Research |year=2004 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/resrep02029.9}}</ref>

Besides fruit, the tree yields valuable wood and hard seeds which are burned for fuel, and has parts used [[herbalism|medicinally]] in [[Vietnam]] and [[Tibet]].<ref name=poudel/>

[[Catechin-7-O-glucoside]] can be found in the stem barks of ''C. axillaris''.<ref>Flavanoidal constituents of ''Choerospondias axillaries'' and their in vitro antitumor and anti-hypoxia activities. Li Chang-wei, Cui Cheng-bin, Cai Bing, Han Bing, Li Ming-ming and Fan Ming, Chinese Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, 2009, 19 (1), pages 48-51,64 ([http://www.zgyhzz.cn/qikan/epaper/zhaiyao.asp?bsid=14526 abstract] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140309191625/http://www.zgyhzz.cn/qikan/epaper/zhaiyao.asp?bsid=14526 |date=2014-03-09 }})</ref>
